title: Two-Phase Commit (2PC)
body:
# Two-Phase Commit (2PC)

<BurgerAnalogy text={"Suppose the digital systems at our burger restaurant must reserve inventory and record a charge in one coordinated transaction. A coordinator first asks both participants to prepare, then records and communicates the final decision. This illustrates two-phase commit for participating transactional systems; it does not make grilling or courier travel reversible, and prepared participants may block if the coordinator becomes unavailable."} />

Understand how Two-Phase Commit coordinates a single commit-or-abort decision across participating transactional systems.

## Overview

<Cards cols={2}>

<Card title="Phase 1: Prepare" accent="brand">

The coordinator asks all participants to prepare for the transaction. Each participant checks whether it can commit, durably records its prepared state before voting yes, and holds the resources required to honor the final decision.

</Card>

<Card title="Phase 2: Commit" accent="green">

The coordinator durably records commit only if every participant votes yes; otherwise it decides abort. It communicates that decision, which prepared participants must follow and recover after failures.

</Card>

</Cards>

## Characteristics

<Cards cols={2}>

<Card title="Advantages" accent="brand">

- Coordinates one atomic commit-or-abort outcome
- Prevents partial transactions
- Transparent decision-making process
- Atomic commitment under the protocol's recovery assumptions
- Can work with a transaction manager and separate isolation mechanisms

</Card>

<Card title="Limitations" accent="red">

- Blocking (participants wait for decision)
- Sensitive to coordinator failures
- Higher latency due to two phases
- Communication overhead
- Possibility of deadlocks

</Card>

</Cards>

## Use Cases

<Cards cols={3}>

<Card title="Banking Systems" accent="brand">

Coordinated updates across transactional account stores that support the protocol. External banks or payment APIs cannot participate atomically unless they expose compatible transactional interfaces.

</Card>

<Card title="E-commerce" accent="purple">

Order-record and inventory updates can commit together or abort together when all stores participate. Cooking, courier travel and ordinary payment APIs are not automatically covered; these workflows often require a saga instead.

</Card>

<Card title="Reservations" accent="green">

Hotel, flight, or event reservation systems that must coordinate multiple resources simultaneously.

</Card>

</Cards>
